subject: Physics
title: Rohan's Market Quest: Measuring the World
hook: A shopkeeper's scales, a surveyor's tape, and why the whole world agrees on how to measure.

slides.title: Units and Measurements
slides.storyContext: Rohan visits the local vegetable market with his teacher Mr. Sharma and discovers why measurement matters.

slides.title: The Market Mystery
slides.storyContext: Rohan asks Anaya at the market: 'Why does your dad's scale show 1 kg, but the digital one shows 1000 grams?' Anaya's confused. Mr. Sharma steps in: 'Different units, same quantity. But here's the catch—if every shop used different units, chaos!' Rohan realizes: the whole world needs to agree on how to measure.

slides.title: What is a Unit?
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma draws a line in the sand: 'A unit is a standard quantity we use to measure things.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: A unit is a standard quantity adopted by convention to measure a physical quantity.

points.label: Why?
points.text: Without units, '5' means nothing. 5 kg sugar ≠ 5 meters of rope ≠ 5 seconds of time.

points.label: Example
points.text: Length: meter (m), mass: kilogram (kg), time: second (s).

slides.inSimpleWords: A unit is like the answer to 'measuring what?' — it tells you if you're measuring kilos, meters, or seconds.

slides.title: The SI Base Units (International Standard)
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma pulls out a reference card: 'In 1960, the world agreed on 7 fundamental units called SI base units. Every physical quantity is built from these 7.'

points.label: The 7 SI Base Units
points.text: Length (meter, m), Mass (kilogram, kg), Time (second, s), Current (ampere, A), Temperature (kelvin, K), Luminous intensity (candela, cd), Mole (mol).

points.label: Why SI?
points.text: Système International d'Unités — used by scientists worldwide. Ensures consistency.

points.label: Daily use in India
points.text: When you buy rice by kg, cook for minutes, measure cloth by meters—you are using SI.

slides.inSimpleWords: The whole world uses the same 7 building blocks to measure everything—like how all LEGO sets use the same-sized bricks.

slides.title: Prefixes: Making Big and Small Numbers Easy
slides.storyContext: Rohan asks: 'Why do we say 1000 meters is 1 kilometer, not just 1000 meters?' Mr. Sharma smiles: 'Prefixes are shortcuts for big and small numbers.'

points.label: Large prefixes
points.text: kilo (k) = 10³, mega (M) = 10⁶, giga (G) = 10⁹, tera (T) = 10¹².

points.label: Small prefixes
points.text: milli (m) = 10⁻³, micro (μ) = 10⁻⁶, nano (n) = 10⁻⁹, pico (p) = 10⁻¹².

points.label: Real Indian examples
points.text: Your phone: gigabytes of data, nanoseconds to process. Monsoon rainfall: millimeters or centimeters. Distance to school: kilometers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Prefixes are labels that multiply the unit. 1 km = 1000 m (kilo means ×1000).

slides.title: Measurement Error & Significant Figures
slides.storyContext: Anaya's father measures sugar on an old scale (±50 g uncertainty) and a new digital scale (±1 g). Rohan asks: 'Which is correct?' Mr. Sharma: 'Both are, but one is more precise. And we only report as many digits as we can trust.'

points.label: Systematic error
points.text: The scale's zero mark is off—every reading is 10 g too high (always the same error).

points.label: Random error
points.text: The scale jiggles a bit—sometimes you read 100 g, sometimes 101 g.

points.label: Significant figures
points.text: Write only the digits you trust. If your scale reads ±1 g, write 250 g (3 sig figs), not 250.00 g (5 sig figs).

slides.inSimpleWords: Every measurement has tiny errors. Significant figures are the digits you can trust—don't pretend you're more precise than you really are.

slides.title: Dimensional Analysis & Unit Conversion
slides.storyContext: Rohan needs to convert the market's rice price from rupees per kilogram to rupees per gram. Mr. Sharma teaches him a trick: treat units like numbers in a fraction.

points.label: The trick
points.text: Multiply by a conversion factor = 1. E.g., 1 kg = 1000 g, so (1 kg)/(1000 g) = 1.

points.label: Example
points.text: 100 rupees/kg = 100 rupees/kg × (1 kg)/(1000 g) = 0.1 rupees/g.

points.label: Dimensional check
points.text: Always cancel units. If you end with wrong units (e.g., m/kg when you want m/s), you made an error.

slides.inSimpleWords: To convert units, multiply by a fraction that equals 1. The unwanted units cancel, and only the units you want remain.

slides.title: Worked Example: Density Calculation
slides.storyContext: Anaya's father wants to know the density of his cooking oil. He fills a 1-liter bottle (volume = 1000 cm³) and weighs it on the market scale: 920 g (not counting the bottle).

example.problem: Calculate the density of cooking oil in kg/m³. Given: mass = 920 g, volume = 1000 cm³.
example.solution: Step 1: Convert to SI units. Mass = 920 g = 0.92 kg; Volume = 1000 cm³ = 1000 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 10⁻³ m³. Step 2: Density = mass/volume = 0.92 kg / 10⁻³ m³ = 920 kg/m³.

slides.inSimpleWords: Oil is lighter than water (which has density 1000 kg/m³), so oil floats—and our calculation confirms it: 920 < 1000.

slides.title: Your Turn: Convert Rainfall
slides.storyContext: During monsoon, Mr. Sharma tells Rohan: 'The forecast says 45 mm of rain will fall. If our roof is 10 m², how many liters of water will we collect?' (Hint: 1 m³ = 1000 L.)

example.problem: Calculate the volume of rainwater collected on a 10 m² roof with 45 mm of rainfall.
example.solution: Step 1: Convert depth to meters: 45 mm = 45 × 10⁻³ m = 0.045 m. Step 2: Volume = area × depth = 10 m² × 0.045 m = 0.45 m³. Step 3: Convert to liters: 0.45 m³ × 1000 L/m³ = 450 L.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rainfall depth × roof area = volume of water you can collect and store.

slides.title: What You've Learned
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma summarizes as they leave the market: 'Measurement connects theory to reality. Without agreed units and careful technique, physics is just stories.'

points.text: A unit is a standard quantity for measuring physical quantities.
The 7 SI base units (meter, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, candela, mole) are the foundation.
Prefixes (kilo-, milli-, micro-, etc.) make large and small numbers easy to write.
Errors exist; significant figures show precision. Don't claim more accuracy than you have.
Dimensional analysis and unit conversion are the tools to get right answers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Measurement is the language of physics. Learn the SI units, be honest about precision, and always check your units when converting.

subject: Physics
title: Priya's Delhi Metro Journey: Velocity, Acceleration, and Graphs
hook: A commute on the world's fastest metro reveals how to describe and predict motion mathematically.

slides.title: Motion in a Straight Line
slides.storyContext: Priya rides Delhi Metro from her home to her physics coaching. Coach Vikram sits beside her with a stopwatch, turning a simple commute into a physics lesson.

slides.title: The Metro's Secret
slides.storyContext: As the metro accelerates smoothly from the station, Coach Vikram asks Priya: 'Feel that push in your back? That's acceleration. In 30 seconds, we go from 0 to 80 km/h. Can you predict our speed at 15 seconds?' Priya realizes: if she knows how velocity changes, she can predict the future.

slides.title: Distance, Displacement & Speed, Velocity
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram explains: 'You walked to the metro station (400 m away), but if I ask your displacement, it's the straight-line distance from home to station—only 300 m, because the path wasn't straight.'

points.label: Distance
points.text: Total path length (always positive). You walked 400 m, so distance = 400 m.

points.label: Displacement
points.text: Straight-line change from start to finish, with direction. From home to station = 300 m North.

points.label: Speed
points.text: Scalar: distance/time. You covered 400 m in 5 minutes, so speed = 400/300 = 1.33 m/s.

points.label: Velocity
points.text: Vector: displacement/time. Displacement 300 m / 5 min = 1 m/s North.

slides.inSimpleWords: Distance is 'how far you traveled'; displacement is 'how far you ended up from where you started.' Speed doesn't care about direction; velocity does.

slides.title: Acceleration: The Rate of Change of Velocity
slides.storyContext: The metro leaves the station. At 0 s, speed = 0 m/s. At 10 s, speed = 5 m/s. At 20 s, speed = 10 m/s. Coach Vikram asks: 'What's the pattern?'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Acceleration a = Δv / Δt (change in velocity divided by time taken).

points.label: For the metro
points.text: In the first 20 seconds, velocity changed by 10 m/s, so a = 10/20 = 0.5 m/s².

points.label: Direction matters
points.text: If speed increases, acceleration is positive (same direction as motion). If speed decreases (braking), acceleration is negative (opposite to motion).

slides.inSimpleWords: Acceleration tells you how fast your speed is changing. A car speeding up or slowing down is accelerating.

slides.title: Kinematic Equations for Constant Acceleration
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram pulls out a notebook: 'If acceleration is constant (like the metro's smooth start), we can use three magic formulas to find distance, velocity, or time—even without a stopwatch.'

points.label: Equation 1
points.text: v = u + at (final velocity = initial velocity + acceleration × time)

points.label: Equation 2
points.text: s = ut + ½at² (distance = initial velocity × time + ½ × acceleration × time²)

points.label: Equation 3
points.text: v² = u² + 2as (final velocity² = initial velocity² + 2 × acceleration × distance)

points.label: Symbols
points.text: u = initial velocity, v = final velocity, a = acceleration, t = time, s = distance.

slides.inSimpleWords: These three equations connect velocity, acceleration, distance, and time. Pick which ones you know, and solve for what you want.

slides.title: Position-Time & Velocity-Time Graphs
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram draws two graphs on his notebook. The first shows the metro's position over time (curved, because acceleration). The second shows velocity over time (a straight line, because constant acceleration).

points.label: s-t graph (position vs time)
points.text: Slope = velocity. Curved graph = acceleration changing. Straight line = constant velocity.

points.label: v-t graph (velocity vs time)
points.text: Slope = acceleration. Area under the curve = displacement. Straight line = constant acceleration.

points.label: For the metro
points.text: v-t graph starts at (0, 0), rises in a straight line to (20 s, 10 m/s). Slope = 0.5 m/s². Area = ½ × 20 × 10 = 100 m traveled.

slides.inSimpleWords: Graphs are shortcuts to see the story of motion. Position graph's slope = velocity. Velocity graph's slope = acceleration; area = distance.

slides.title: Free Fall: Motion Under Gravity Alone
slides.storyContext: At a tunnel entrance, a tunnel worker drops a tool. Coach Vikram: 'On Earth, gravity gives every object the same acceleration downward: g = 9.8 m/s². That's free fall. Air resistance doesn't exist in our ideal world—yet.'

points.label: Acceleration due to gravity
points.text: g = 9.8 m/s² (≈ 10 m/s² in quick math). Direction: downward (toward Earth's center).

points.label: Free fall equations
points.text: Same as kinematic equations, but a is always g (or −g if up is positive). h = ½gt² for distance fallen from rest.

points.label: Example: 1-second rule
points.text: Drop a ball from rest. At t = 1 s, distance fallen = ½ × 10 × 1² = 5 m. At t = 2 s, distance = ½ × 10 × 4 = 20 m.

slides.inSimpleWords: In free fall, acceleration is always 9.8 m/s² downward. Heavier and lighter objects fall at the same rate (in a vacuum).

slides.title: Worked Example: Metro Acceleration
slides.storyContext: The metro starts from rest and accelerates at 0.5 m/s² for 20 seconds, then moves at constant velocity. Priya asks: 'How far did we travel during acceleration?'

example.problem: A metro train starts from rest (u = 0) and accelerates at a = 0.5 m/s² for t = 20 seconds. Find (1) final velocity and (2) distance traveled.

slides.inSimpleWords: In 20 seconds, the metro reaches 10 m/s and covers 100 meters—that's the length of the platform!

slides.title: Your Turn: Braking Problem
slides.storyContext: The metro approaches Rajiv Chowk station traveling at 15 m/s. The driver applies brakes with a deceleration of −2.5 m/s². Priya asks: 'How long until we stop, and how far does the train travel while braking?'

example.problem: A train moving at u = 15 m/s applies brakes (a = −2.5 m/s²). Find time to stop and distance during braking.
example.solution: Using v = u + at (final velocity v = 0): 0 = 15 + (−2.5)t → t = 6 seconds. Using s = ut + ½at²: s = 15(6) + ½(−2.5)(36) = 90 − 45 = 45 m.

slides.inSimpleWords: The train brakes for 6 seconds and travels 45 meters—almost the length of a cricket pitch!

slides.title: What You've Learned
slides.storyContext: As Priya steps off at her coaching center, Coach Vikram reminds her: 'Motion isn't random—it follows rules. Velocity, acceleration, and the kinematic equations tie them together.'

points.text: Displacement is a vector (with direction); distance is a scalar.
Velocity = displacement/time; speed = distance/time. Velocity is a vector.
Acceleration = change in velocity / time. It can be positive (speeding up) or negative (slowing down).
Three kinematic equations describe motion with constant acceleration: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as.
Graphs (s-t and v-t) show motion visually. Slope and area have physical meaning.
Free fall: g = 9.8 m/s² acts on all objects equally.

slides.inSimpleWords: Motion is predictable when acceleration is constant. Learn the equations, draw the graphs, and you can forecast where and when.

subject: Physics
title: Arjun's Cricket Shot: Projectile Motion in 2D
hook: A cricket ball soars in an arc, and math explains why—vectors, components, and the beauty of parabolas.

slides.title: Motion in a Plane
slides.storyContext: At the cricket ground, Arjun hits a six. Coach Deepak asks: 'Can you predict where the ball lands?' The answer lies in 2D motion.

slides.title: The Cricket Ball's Secret
slides.storyContext: Arjun's hit launches the ball at 20 m/s at 45° to the horizontal. Coach Deepak stops him: 'Before you celebrate, let's break that into two parts: horizontal motion (constant velocity) and vertical motion (free fall under gravity). Together, they make a parabola.'

slides.title: Vectors & Components: Breaking Motion into Parts
slides.storyContext: Coach Deepak draws a right triangle: 'The ball's initial velocity (20 m/s at 45°) has two components: horizontal and vertical. Each acts independently.'

points.label: Component breakdown
points.text: For velocity v at angle θ: horizontal component vₓ = v cos(θ); vertical component vᵧ = v sin(θ).

points.label: Independence principle
points.text: Horizontal motion is unaffected by gravity. Vertical motion follows free-fall rules independently.

slides.inSimpleWords: A diagonal velocity can be split into horizontal (left-right) and vertical (up-down) parts. They don't interfere with each other.

slides.title: Projectile Motion: The Two-Axis Approach
slides.storyContext: Coach Deepak pulls out a whiteboard: 'Treat horizontal and vertical motion separately, using the equations you know from straight-line motion.'

points.label: Horizontal (x-direction)
points.text: No gravity here. Acceleration aₓ = 0. Velocity vₓ is constant. Distance x = vₓ × t.

points.label: Vertical (y-direction)
points.text: Gravity acts. Acceleration aᵧ = −g = −9.8 m/s². Use kinematic equations: vᵧ = vᵧ₀ − gt; y = vᵧ₀t − ½gt².

points.label: Combined motion
points.text: At time t, the ball is at (x, y) = (vₓt, vᵧ₀t − ½gt²). This gives a parabolic path.

slides.inSimpleWords: Horizontal motion is simple: distance = speed × time. Vertical motion is free fall (gravity pulls down). Both happen at the same time.

slides.title: Range & Maximum Height
slides.storyContext: Zara (fielding) stands far away. Coach asks: 'Where will Arjun's ball land? And at what point is it highest?' He derives two formulas.

points.label: Maximum height H
points.text: The ball reaches maximum height when vᵧ = 0. Using vᵧ = vᵧ₀ − gt: t_max = vᵧ₀/g. Then H = vᵧ₀²/(2g).

points.label: For Arjun's shot
points.text: vᵧ₀ = 14.14 m/s. H = (14.14)² / (2 × 9.8) = 200/19.6 ≈ 10.2 m. The ball reaches 10 meters high!

points.label: Range R
points.text: Total time of flight: ball returns when y = 0, so t_total = 2vᵧ₀/g. Range R = vₓ × t_total = (v²/g) sin(2θ).

points.label: For 45° angle
points.text: R = (20²/9.8) sin(90°) = 400/9.8 ≈ 40.8 m. The ball lands about 41 meters away—a huge six!

slides.inSimpleWords: The highest point is where upward velocity becomes zero. Range is how far it travels before hitting the ground.

slides.title: Time of Flight & Trajectory Equation
slides.storyContext: Coach Deepak asks: 'How long is the ball in the air? And can we write y as a function of x (the ball's path)?'

points.label: Time of flight
points.text: The ball leaves the ground (y = 0) and returns at y = 0. Solving 0 = vᵧ₀t − ½gt²: t = 0 (start) or t = 2vᵧ₀/g (landing).

points.label: For Arjun's shot
points.text: t = 2 × 14.14 / 9.8 ≈ 2.89 seconds. The ball is in the air for nearly 3 seconds.

points.label: Trajectory equation
points.text: Eliminating t from x = vₓt and y = vᵧ₀t − ½gt²: y = x tan(θ) − [gx²/(2v² cos²θ)]. A parabola!

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: The ball rises (tan term dominates), then falls (−gx²/... term dominates). A perfect arc.

slides.inSimpleWords: The ball stays airborne for 2-3 seconds and traces a parabola—up, then down. The math describes the arc perfectly.

slides.title: Relative Motion: The Fielder's Perspective
slides.storyContext: Zara is running after the ball. Coach Deepak asks: 'From Zara's moving viewpoint, the ball looks different than from the stand.'

points.label: Relative velocity
points.text: If Zara runs at vz = 5 m/s and the ball moves at vb = 14.14 m/s (horizontal), relative velocity = vb − vz = 9.14 m/s.

points.label: Why it matters
points.text: To catch the ball, Zara sees it moving at relative velocity, not ground velocity. Misjudging means a missed catch.

points.label: 3D extension
points.text: In real cricket, the ball also rotates (spin), changing air resistance. 2D analysis is the foundation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Motion looks different depending on who's watching. A fielder running toward the ball sees it approaching faster than a spectator does.

slides.title: Worked Example: The Six
slides.storyContext: Arjun launches the ball at 25 m/s at 30° to the horizontal. Find maximum height, range, and time of flight.

example.problem: A cricket ball is hit at initial velocity v = 25 m/s, angle θ = 30°. Find (1) maximum height, (2) range, and (3) time of flight.

slides.inSimpleWords: A 30° launch angle gives a 55-meter range and about 8 meters height—a powerful six down the ground!

slides.title: Your Turn: Circular Motion (Bonus)
slides.storyContext: Coach Deepak extends the idea: 'Projectile motion is half of circular motion. In uniform circular motion, acceleration is constant (toward center) but velocity is always tangential. Can you describe it?'

example.problem: A ball moves in a circle of radius r = 2 m at speed v = 6 m/s. Find centripetal acceleration and period.
example.solution: Centripetal acceleration a_c = v²/r = (6)²/2 = 18 m/s² (toward center). Period T = 2πr/v = 2π(2)/6 ≈ 2.09 seconds (time for one full lap).

slides.inSimpleWords: In circular motion, the ball's direction changes constantly, so there's always acceleration pointing toward the center—even though speed is constant.

slides.title: What You've Learned
slides.storyContext: The match ends. Arjun's six flew beautifully into the crowd. Coach Deepak smiles: 'That arc you saw? Pure physics.'

points.text: 2D motion can be split into independent horizontal and vertical components.
Horizontal motion has constant velocity (no gravity). Vertical motion is free fall.
Maximum height H = v₀ᵧ²/(2g); Range R = (v₀²/g) sin(2θ); Time of flight t = 2v₀ᵧ/g.
The trajectory is parabolic: y = x tan(θ) − gx²/(2v₀² cos²θ).
Relative motion: velocity depends on the observer's frame of reference.
Circular motion is a special case where centripetal acceleration a_c = v²/r points inward.

slides.inSimpleWords: Projectile motion is elegant: split the velocity into parts, treat each axis separately, combine at the end. The result is always a parabola.

subject: Physics
title: Kabir's Auto-Rickshaw Ride: Newton's Laws Explained
hook: Why does a rickshaw suddenly jerk when the driver accelerates? Three laws of motion—Newton's gift to physics.

slides.title: Laws of Motion
slides.storyContext: Kabir and Ankita ride an auto-rickshaw through Delhi traffic. Driver Uncle explains motion without knowing Newton's laws—but physics is happening.

slides.title: The Rickshaw Puzzle
slides.storyContext: The rickshaw is parked. Kabir asks Driver Uncle: 'Why doesn't the rickshaw move unless you accelerate it?' Driver Uncle scratches his head: 'That's just how it is.' Ankita jumps in: 'No, it's Newton! Things want to stay at rest. It's called inertia.' Kabir realizes: there's a law here.

slides.title: Newton's First Law: Inertia
slides.storyContext: Kabir sketches on paper: 'If no force acts on an object, it stays at rest or in motion forever. Inertia is resistance to change.'

points.label: The law
points.text: An object in motion stays in motion, and an object at rest stays at rest, unless acted upon by an external force.

points.label: Inertia
points.text: The natural tendency of an object to resist changes in motion. Mass is the measure of inertia.

points.label: Why the rickshaw jerks
points.text: When Driver Uncle suddenly accelerates, Kabir's body wants to stay at rest (inertia), so he feels pushed backward. When he brakes, he wants to keep moving forward.

points.label: Real-world examples
points.text: Passengers lurch when the train stops. Your phone slides on the car seat when the car turns. A coin falls straight down when you pull a tablecloth.

slides.inSimpleWords: Objects resist change. Once moving, they want to keep moving. At rest, they want to stay at rest. That's inertia.

slides.title: Newton's Second Law: F = ma
slides.storyContext: Driver Uncle steps on the gas. Ankita asks: 'How hard he pushes matters, right?' Kabir replies: 'Yes! The engine's force determines the acceleration. That's F = ma.'

points.label: The law
points.text: Net force = mass × acceleration. F_net = ma. Force, mass, and acceleration are linked mathematically.

points.label: Force is a vector
points.text: 1 newton (N) is the force needed to accelerate 1 kg at 1 m/s². 1 N = 1 kg⋅m/s².

points.label: For the rickshaw
points.text: Engine produces force F. Rickshaw mass m ≈ 1000 kg. If F = 5000 N, then a = F/m = 5000/1000 = 5 m/s². Gentle acceleration.

points.label: Multiple forces
points.text: Net force = sum of all forces. If engine pushes with 5000 N and friction opposes with 2000 N, net F = 3000 N.

slides.inSimpleWords: Force causes acceleration. The more force, the more acceleration. The more massive the object, the less acceleration for the same force.

slides.title: Newton's Third Law: Action & Reaction
slides.storyContext: The rickshaw pushes forward on the road. Ankita asks: 'Does the road push back?' Kabir nods: 'Yes! The road pushes the rickshaw forward. That's Newton's third law.'

points.label: The law
points.text: For every action, there's an equal and opposite reaction. If A exerts force on B, then B exerts equal force on A (in opposite direction).

points.label: For the rickshaw
points.text: Wheels push backward on the road (action). Road pushes forward on wheels (reaction). This forward push accelerates the rickshaw.

points.label: Why both don't cancel
points.text: Action and reaction act on different objects (road and rickshaw). Newton's 2nd law applies separately to each.

points.label: Daily examples
points.text: Jump: you push Earth down, Earth pushes you up. Swim: push water backward, water pushes you forward. Throw: you push ball, ball pushes your hand.

slides.inSimpleWords: Forces always come in pairs. If you push on something, it pushes back with equal strength—just in the opposite direction.

slides.title: Types of Forces: Friction, Normal, Tension
slides.storyContext: The rickshaw slows down as traffic thickens. Kabir lists the forces: 'Brakes create friction. The seat holds us up (normal force). The rope tying luggage on top is under tension.'

points.label: Friction
points.text: Opposes motion. Kinetic friction f_k = μ_k × N (μ_k is coefficient, N is normal force). For the rickshaw: brakes create high friction.

points.label: Normal force
points.text: Perpendicular contact force. On level ground, N = mg (weight). The ground pushes up on Kabir with N = his weight.

points.label: Tension
points.text: Force in ropes/cables. A rope holding luggage is under tension T, pulling at both ends equally.

points.label: Weight
points.text: Gravitational force: W = mg (mass × gravity). Kabir's weight = 60 kg × 10 m/s² = 600 N downward.

slides.inSimpleWords: Friction slows things down. Normal force is the 'push' supporting weight. Tension is the 'pull' in ropes. Weight is gravity pulling down.

slides.title: Applications: Inclines, Pulleys, and Elevators
slides.storyContext: The rickshaw climbs a slope toward a temple. Kabir realizes: 'The component of weight along the slope opposes motion. We're working against gravity.'

points.label: Inclined plane
points.text: Weight W = mg acts downward. Component parallel to slope: W_|| = mg sin(θ). Component perpendicular: W_⊥ = mg cos(θ). Friction opposes W_||.

points.label: For a 30° slope
points.text: W_|| = 100 kg × 10 × sin(30°) = 100 × 10 × 0.5 = 500 N pulling the rickshaw downhill.

points.label: Pulley systems
points.text: A rope over a pulley transmits tension. If mechanical advantage = 4, a 100 N pull lifts 400 N weight.

points.label: Elevator
points.text: When accelerating upward, normal force N > mg (you feel heavier). When accelerating downward, N < mg (lighter).

slides.inSimpleWords: On slopes, gravity has a component pulling downhill. Pulleys can amplify force. Elevators play tricks with normal force—making you feel heavier or lighter.

slides.title: Worked Example: Rickshaw Braking
slides.storyContext: The rickshaw is moving at 10 m/s. Sudden red light! Driver Uncle brakes hard. Friction force f = 4000 N. Mass of rickshaw + passengers = 1200 kg. Find deceleration and stopping distance.

example.problem: A rickshaw (m = 1200 kg) moving at v = 10 m/s brakes with friction force f = 4000 N. Find deceleration and stopping distance.
example.solution: Step 1: Using F = ma, deceleration a = −F/m = −4000/1200 = −3.33 m/s² (negative because it opposes motion). Step 2: Using v² = u² + 2as (with final v = 0): 0 = 10² + 2(−3.33)s → s = 100/6.66 ≈ 15 meters. The rickshaw stops in 15 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Strong braking (4000 N force) on a heavy rickshaw (1200 kg) creates a deceleration of 3.33 m/s² and stops it in 15 meters—about the length of a bus.

slides.title: Your Turn: Connected Masses
slides.storyContext: Two rickshaws are tied together (tension T in the rope). The first (m₁ = 1000 kg) is pulled by an engine with force F = 5000 N. The second (m₂ = 800 kg) is towed. Find acceleration and tension in the rope.

example.problem: Two connected masses: m₁ = 1000 kg (pulled by F = 5000 N), m₂ = 800 kg (towed). Find system acceleration and tension T in rope.
example.solution: Step 1: System acceleration a = F_total / m_total = 5000 / (1000 + 800) = 5000/1800 ≈ 2.78 m/s². Step 2: For the second rickshaw alone: T = m₂ × a = 800 × 2.78 ≈ 2222 N. The rope must pull with 2222 N to accelerate the second rickshaw.

slides.inSimpleWords: When masses are connected, they accelerate together. The tension in the connecting rope is just enough to pull the trailing mass.

slides.title: What You've Learned
slides.storyContext: The rickshaw reaches the destination safely. Driver Uncle smiles: 'All that math, and it's just driving!'

points.text: Newton's 1st Law: Objects resist change in motion (inertia). No net force = no acceleration.
Newton's 2nd Law: F_net = ma. Force causes acceleration. Bigger force = bigger acceleration (for same mass).
Newton's 3rd Law: Action and reaction are equal and opposite, acting on different objects.
Common forces: friction (opposes motion), normal force (supports weight), tension (pulls), weight (gravity).
On inclines, weight has components parallel and perpendicular to the slope.
For connected objects, find acceleration of the system, then use it for each object.

slides.inSimpleWords: Newton's laws connect force, mass, and acceleration. They explain why rickshaws jerk, why brakes work, why ropes tighten—everything moves according to these three laws.

subject: Physics
title: Maya's Farm: Why Work & Energy Matter
hook: A farmer pumps water uphill. The work done, energy stored, and power output tell the whole story.

slides.title: Work, Energy and Power
slides.storyContext: On a rural farm in Punjab, Maya helps her father pump water to irrigate the fields. A physics teacher visits and sees a lesson in energy.

slides.title: The Farmer's Wisdom
slides.storyContext: Father pumps water from a well 10 meters deep. Maya asks: 'Does it matter how fast you pump?' Father replies: 'Slower is less tiring, but takes longer.' The Teacher arrives and says: 'That's the difference between work and power. Work is done; power is the rate of doing work.'

slides.title: Work: Force & Displacement
slides.storyContext: The Teacher draws a diagram: 'Work is done when a force moves an object. But only the force component along the displacement counts.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Work W = F · s = F × s × cos(θ), where θ is the angle between force and displacement.

points.label: Unit
points.text: 1 joule (J) = 1 newton × 1 meter (N·m). 1 J is the work done by 1 N force over 1 m.

points.label: For the pump
points.text: Father lifts water mass m = 100 kg upward 10 m against gravity. Force = weight W = mg = 100 × 10 = 1000 N (downward). He applies F = 1000 N upward (opposite). Work = 1000 × 10 × cos(0°) = 10,000 J = 10 kJ.

points.label: No work if perpendicular
points.text: If force is perpendicular to motion (θ = 90°), cos(90°) = 0, so W = 0. Carrying a bucket horizontally does no work (gravity is perpendicular).

slides.inSimpleWords: Work is force times distance, but only the force in the direction of motion counts. Lifting upward does work against gravity; moving sideways at the same height does no work.

slides.title: Energy: Kinetic & Potential
slides.storyContext: The Teacher explains: 'Energy is the capacity to do work. Two types: kinetic (motion) and potential (position).'

points.label: Kinetic energy KE
points.text: Energy of motion: KE = ½ m v². Unit: joules (J). If water flows at 2 m/s, KE = ½ × 100 × 2² = 200 J.

points.label: Gravitational potential energy PE
points.text: Energy of height: PE = mgh (relative to a reference). Water 10 m up: PE = 100 × 10 × 10 = 10,000 J.

points.label: Elastic potential energy
points.text: Energy stored in stretched springs: PE = ½ k x² (k = spring constant, x = compression/extension).

points.label: Total mechanical energy
points.text: E_total = KE + PE. At the top of the well, water has only PE. As it falls, PE converts to KE.

slides.inSimpleWords: Kinetic energy is energy of motion (KE = ½mv²). Potential energy is energy of height (PE = mgh). They can trade places: lift something high (gain PE), let it fall (PE → KE).

slides.title: Conservation of Energy & Work-Energy Theorem
slides.storyContext: Maya watches water flow downhill from the raised tank. 'Where does the energy go?' The Teacher smiles: 'It's conserved—kinetic, potential, and heat from friction all add up to the work you did pumping.'

points.label: Energy conservation
points.text: Total mechanical energy = constant (no friction). KE + PE = constant. As height decreases, speed increases (PE → KE).

points.label: Work-energy theorem
points.text: Work done by net force = change in kinetic energy. W_net = ΔKE = ½m(v_f² − v_i²).

points.label: With friction
points.text: Work by all forces (including friction) = change in KE. W_applied − W_friction = ΔKE. Energy is lost as heat (thermal energy).

points.label: For the farm
points.text: Work pumped = 10 kJ. If no losses, this equals the water's PE at the top. In reality, friction in the pump wastes some energy as heat.

slides.inSimpleWords: Energy can't be created or destroyed, only changed form. Pumping adds energy; friction removes it. The net work determines change in kinetic energy.

slides.title: Power: Rate of Doing Work
slides.storyContext: Father pumps for 10 seconds. Maya asks: 'Does speed matter?' Teacher replies: 'Yes! Power is work per unit time.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Power P = Work / time = W / t. Unit: 1 watt (W) = 1 joule per second (J/s). 1 kilowatt (kW) = 1000 W.

points.label: For the pump
points.text: Work = 10,000 J. If pumped in 10 s, power P = 10,000 / 10 = 1000 W = 1 kW. If in 20 s, P = 500 W.

points.label: Instantaneous power
points.text: P = F · v = F × v × cos(θ). If force and velocity are in the same direction, P = F × v.

points.label: Real-world units
points.text: Electric bulb: 60 W (uses 60 J per second). Car engine: 50 kW. Heavy industry: megawatts (MW). Farm pump: typically 0.5−2 kW.

slides.inSimpleWords: Power is how fast work is done. 1 watt = 1 joule per second. A faster pump does the same work in less time, so higher power.

slides.title: Collisions & Momentum (Bonus: Energy Perspective)
slides.storyContext: A stone falls into the tank. Water splashes. Teacher explains: 'In collisions, momentum is conserved. Kinetic energy might not be (some becomes heat, sound, deformation).'

points.label: Elastic collision
points.text: Both momentum and KE are conserved. Billiard balls bouncing: they rebound with minimal energy loss.

points.label: Inelastic collision
points.text: Momentum is conserved, but KE is not. Objects may stick together, and energy is lost as heat/deformation. Car crash: energy becomes crumpling metal and heat.

points.label: Perfectly inelastic
points.text: Objects stick together. Maximum KE loss (becomes internal energy). Example: mud hitting a wall.

slides.inSimpleWords: In collisions, momentum (mass × velocity) is always conserved. Kinetic energy might be lost (as heat, sound, deformation) in inelastic collisions.

slides.title: Worked Example: Lifting Water
slides.storyContext: Father pumps 1000 kg of water from a 15 m deep well in 30 seconds. Find work done, potential energy gained, and power.

example.problem: A pump lifts 1000 kg water from a 15 m deep well in 30 seconds. Find: (1) work done, (2) PE gained, (3) power.
example.solution: Step 1: Work against gravity W = mgh = 1000 × 10 × 15 = 150,000 J = 150 kJ. Step 2: PE gained = mgh = 150,000 J (same as work, assuming no friction). Step 3: Power P = W/t = 150,000 / 30 = 5000 W = 5 kW.

slides.inSimpleWords: Pumping 1000 kg up 15 meters requires 150 kilojoules of work. If done in 30 seconds, the power is 5 kilowatts—a substantial farm pump!

slides.title: Your Turn: Spring Potential Energy
slides.storyContext: A farmer uses a spring-loaded water pump (spring constant k = 2000 N/m). He compresses the spring by 0.1 m and releases it to lift water. Find elastic PE and the water's speed if it gains that energy.

example.problem: Spring compressed by x = 0.1 m, k = 2000 N/m. Elastic PE is converted to water's KE. If water mass m = 0.5 kg, find final speed v.
example.solution: Step 1: Elastic PE = ½kx² = ½ × 2000 × (0.1)² = 1000 × 0.01 = 10 J. Step 2: By energy conservation, KE = PE, so ½mv² = 10 → v² = 20/0.5 = 40 → v = √40 ≈ 6.32 m/s.

slides.inSimpleWords: Compressing a spring by 0.1 m stores 10 joules. When released, that energy converts to kinetic energy, launching water at 6.3 m/s.

slides.title: What You've Learned
slides.storyContext: Sunset on the farm. The tank is full, the crops are happy. Teacher smiles: 'You've done work, and the water has potential energy ready for tomorrow.'

points.text: Work W = F · s · cos(θ). Only the force component along displacement counts.
Kinetic energy KE = ½mv² (energy of motion). Potential energy PE = mgh (energy of height).
Energy is conserved: KE + PE = constant (without friction). With friction, some energy becomes heat.
Work-energy theorem: W_net = ΔKE. Net work equals change in kinetic energy.
Power P = Work / time (or P = F × v). Unit: watt (W) = joule per second.
In collisions, momentum is always conserved. KE might be lost (inelastic) or conserved (elastic).

slides.inSimpleWords: Work is force times distance. Energy is capacity to do work. Power is the rate. Conserve energy: what goes up must come down (or heat up).

subject: Physics
chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
title: Ritesh's Spinning Top: Rigid Bodies & Angular Motion
hook: A top spins, never falling. But when you twist a stick, one end is faster than the other. Why? Rotation is different from translation.

slides.title: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
slides.storyContext: Ritesh spins a wooden top. It wobbles, rights itself, then spins steadily. Professor Anjali watches and begins a lesson about rotation.

slides.title: The Spinning Mystery
slides.storyContext: Ritesh notices: when the top spins fast, it's stable; when slow, it topples. Professor Anjali asks: 'Why does rotation stabilize it?' Priya joins: 'And how is rotation different from translation?' Ritesh realizes: rotation has its own physics, separate from linear motion.

slides.title: Angular Displacement, Velocity & Acceleration
slides.storyContext: Professor draws the top from above. 'Each point on the top moves in a circle. We describe this with angles, not distances.'

points.label: Angular displacement θ
points.text: Measured in radians (rad). Full circle = 2π rad ≈ 6.28 rad. (1 rad = 180°/π ≈ 57.3°.)

points.label: Angular velocity ω
points.text: Rate of angular change: ω = θ/t (radians per second, rad/s). Top spinning 10 rad/s is rotating fast.

points.label: Angular acceleration α
points.text: Rate of change of ω: α = Δω/Δt (rad/s²). Spinning up or slowing down.

points.label: Link to linear motion
points.text: For a point at radius r: linear velocity v = ωr; linear acceleration a = αr. Tip of the top moves faster than its center.

slides.inSimpleWords: Angular quantities (θ, ω, α) describe rotation like linear quantities (s, v, a) describe straight-line motion. Multiply by radius r to convert.

slides.title: Moment of Inertia: Rotational Mass
slides.storyContext: Professor spins a rod from its center, then from its edge. 'It's harder to spin from the edge—the mass is farther away. That's moment of inertia.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: I = Σ m_i r_i² (sum of mass × distance² for each part). Measures resistance to angular acceleration.

points.label: Unit
points.text: kg·m² (kilogram-meter squared).

points.label: Common shapes
points.text: Solid disk/cylinder: I = ½MR². Thin hoop: I = MR². Solid sphere: I = (2/5)MR². Long rod (about center): I = (1/12)ML².

points.label: For the top
points.text: If the top is approximated as a disk (M = 50 g, R = 2 cm), I = ½ × 0.05 × (0.02)² = 10⁻⁵ kg·m².

slides.inSimpleWords: Moment of inertia is how hard it is to spin something. Putting mass far from the axis increases I greatly (because of r²).

slides.title: Torque & Angular Momentum
slides.storyContext: Ritesh applies a force to the top's edge. Professor: 'The force's distance from the axis matters. That's torque—the rotational cousin of force.'

points.label: Torque τ
points.text: τ = r × F = r F sin(θ) (radius × force × sin of angle). Unit: N·m (newton-meter).

points.label: Newton's 2nd law (rotational)
points.text: τ = I α. Torque causes angular acceleration, like force causes linear acceleration.

points.label: Angular momentum L
points.text: L = I ω (inertia × angular velocity). Unit: kg·m²/s. A spinning top has large L.

points.label: Conservation
points.text: If no external torque acts, angular momentum is conserved. Spinning top: no external torque → L is constant → ω is constant (steady spin).

slides.inSimpleWords: Torque is rotational force. The farther from the axis you push, the more torque. Torque causes angular acceleration (τ = Iα). Angular momentum is conserved without external torque.

slides.title: Rotational Kinetic Energy
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'Does a spinning top have energy?' Professor: 'Yes! Rotational KE = ½Iω²—the spinning stores energy just like motion does.'

points.label: Rotational KE
points.text: KE_rot = ½Iω². Similar to linear KE = ½mv², but using I and ω instead of m and v.

points.label: For the top
points.text: I = 10⁻⁵ kg·m², ω = 100 rad/s (fast spin). KE = ½ × 10⁻⁵ × 100² = ½ × 10⁻⁵ × 10,000 = 0.05 J. Small but real.

points.label: Total mechanical energy
points.text: For a rotating object at height h: E_total = KE_linear + KE_rot + PE = ½mv² + ½Iω² + mgh.

points.label: Energy stored
points.text: A spinning flywheel stores rotational KE. Can be converted back to useful work (e.g., regenerative braking in trains).

slides.inSimpleWords: Spinning has kinetic energy just like moving does. A faster spin (larger ω) or larger moment of inertia (I) means more rotational energy.

slides.title: Rolling Without Slipping: Combined Motion
slides.storyContext: A ball rolls down an incline. Priya asks: 'Is it just rotating, or is it also translating?' Professor: 'Both! And there's a constraint: rolling without slipping means v = ωr.'

points.label: Rolling condition
points.text: For no slipping: v_center = ωr (linear velocity of center = angular velocity × radius).

points.label: Total KE
points.text: KE_total = ½mv_center² + ½Iω² = ½mv² + ½I(v/r)². This is split between translation and rotation.

points.label: For a solid sphere
points.text: I = (2/5)mr². So KE = ½mv² + ½(2/5)mr²(v/r)² = ½mv² + (1/5)mv² = (7/10)mv². 70% goes to translation, 30% to rotation.

points.label: Down an incline
points.text: A solid sphere accelerates slower than a sliding block (friction-free) because energy goes into rotation. v_sphere² = (10/7)gh (at bottom), v_block² = 2gh.

slides.inSimpleWords: A rolling ball has two kinds of motion: its center moves forward (translation) and the ball spins (rotation). No slipping means v = ωr.

slides.title: Worked Example: Spinning Top
slides.storyContext: Ritesh spins the top with initial ω = 50 rad/s. Air resistance and friction create a torque τ = −0.001 N·m. If I = 10⁻⁵ kg·m², how long until the top stops?

example.problem: Top: I = 10⁻⁵ kg·m², ω_initial = 50 rad/s, torque τ = −0.001 N·m (due to friction). Find time to stop.
example.solution: Step 1: Angular acceleration α = τ/I = −0.001 / 10⁻⁵ = −100 rad/s². Step 2: Using ω_f = ω_i + αt (with ω_f = 0): 0 = 50 + (−100)t → t = 0.5 s. The top stops in half a second.

slides.inSimpleWords: Friction torque causes the top to decelerate. Angular acceleration = torque/moment of inertia. A small top stops quickly because friction's torque is comparable to its small inertia.

slides.title: Your Turn: Rolling Sphere
slides.storyContext: A solid sphere (mass m = 2 kg, radius r = 0.1 m) rolls down a frictionless 5 m incline (angle 30°). Find final linear velocity at the bottom.

example.problem: Sphere (m = 2 kg, r = 0.1 m) rolls down a frictionless 5 m incline (30° angle). Find v at the bottom. (I_sphere = (2/5)mr².)
example.solution: Step 1: Potential energy PE = mgh = mg(L sin θ) = 2 × 10 × 5 × sin(30°) = 2 × 10 × 5 × 0.5 = 50 J. Step 2: At the bottom, this converts to KE. For rolling: KE = (7/10)mv² = 50 J → v² = 50 × 10 / (7 × 2) = 500/14 ≈ 35.7 → v ≈ 5.98 m/s ≈ 6 m/s.

slides.inSimpleWords: A sphere rolling down 5 meters loses 50 joules of potential energy. Part becomes translational KE, part becomes rotational KE. Final speed is about 6 m/s.

slides.title: What You've Learned
slides.storyContext: The top wobbles to a stop. Ritesh sweeps it off the table. Professor smiles: 'You've seen the full dance—translation and rotation, inertia and torque, energy and momentum.'

points.text: Angular displacement (θ), velocity (ω), and acceleration (α) describe rotation. Related to linear by radius: v = ωr, a = αr.
Moment of inertia I = Σm_ir_i² measures resistance to angular acceleration. I depends on shape and axis.
Torque τ = rF sin(θ) causes angular acceleration: τ = Iα. Angular momentum L = Iω is conserved without external torque.
Rotational kinetic energy KE_rot = ½Iω². Total energy mixes translation, rotation, and potential.
Rolling without slipping: v = ωr. Energy splits between translational and rotational KE.
Center of mass motion (system of particles) follows ΣF_ext = M·a_cm (independent of internal forces).

slides.inSimpleWords: Rotation is a parallel world to translation. Moment of inertia (I) is like mass, torque (τ) is like force, angular momentum (L) is like linear momentum. Conserve energy and momentum.

subject: Physics
title: Advaith's Space Dream: Gravity, Orbits & Black Holes
hook: Why does the Moon orbit Earth? Why doesn't it fall? Newton and Einstein reveal the universe's most elegant law.

slides.title: Gravitation
slides.storyContext: Advaith stares at the Moon during a starry night. Dr. Sharma, who worked at ISRO, steps outside and begins: 'That Moon stays bound by an invisible force—gravity. Let me show you why.'

slides.title: The Moon's Mystery
slides.storyContext: Advaith asks: 'Why doesn't the Moon fall to Earth?' Dr. Sharma smiles: 'It's falling, slowly. Every second, it falls a tiny bit—but Earth's surface curves away at the same rate, so the Moon stays in orbit.' Neha adds: 'That's Newton's genius—gravity is everywhere, pulling all masses toward each other.'

slides.title: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma writes the most important formula: 'Every mass attracts every other mass. The force depends on both masses and their distance.'

points.label: The law
points.text: F = G m₁ m₂ / r² (force = gravitational constant × mass1 × mass2 / distance²)

points.label: Gravitational constant G
points.text: G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg². The same everywhere in the universe.

points.label: Key insight
points.text: Force is proportional to both masses (bigger masses attract more) and inversely proportional to r² (farther apart, weaker attraction).

points.label: Example
points.text: You (m = 60 kg) and Earth (M = 6 × 10²⁴ kg) separated by r = 6.4 × 10⁶ m: F = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 60 × 6 × 10²⁴) / (6.4 × 10⁶)² ≈ 600 N. Your weight!

slides.inSimpleWords: Gravity is mutual: Earth pulls you down, and you pull Earth up (but Earth is too heavy to notice). The larger the masses and the closer together, the stronger the pull.

slides.title: Gravitational Field & g
slides.storyContext: Neha asks: 'Why does a feather fall at the same rate as a stone near Earth?' Dr. Sharma: 'Because gravitational field g = GM/r² is the same for all objects. It's the property of space, not of the falling object.'

points.label: Gravitational field g
points.text: The field strength at distance r from mass M: g = GM/r² (in m/s²). It's the acceleration imparted to any object in the field.

points.label: On Earth's surface
points.text: g = GM_earth / R_earth² = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6 × 10²⁴) / (6.4 × 10⁶)² ≈ 9.8 m/s². Same for all objects.

points.label: Free fall is uniform
points.text: A stone and a feather in vacuum fall at the same acceleration g because they experience the same field, regardless of mass.

points.label: Varying g
points.text: On the Moon (M = 7.3 × 10²², r = 1.7 × 10⁶ m): g_moon ≈ 1.6 m/s². Astronauts are lighter (6 times lighter than on Earth).

slides.inSimpleWords: Gravitational field g is the 'acceleration currency' at a location. Every object in that field experiences g, regardless of its own mass.

slides.title: Escape Velocity & Orbital Motion
slides.storyContext: Advaith asks: 'How fast must a rocket go to escape Earth?' Dr. Sharma draws the energy diagram: 'There are two critical speeds: orbital speed (to circle Earth) and escape velocity (to leave forever).'

points.label: Orbital speed v_orb
points.text: For circular orbit at radius r: gravitational force = centripetal force → GMm/r² = mv²/r → v = √(GM/r).

points.label: For Earth orbit at surface
points.text: v = √(GM/R) = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6 × 10²⁴ / 6.4 × 10⁶) ≈ 7.9 km/s = 7900 m/s. Satellites orbit at this speed.

points.label: Escape velocity v_esc
points.text: To escape, kinetic energy = gravitational potential energy: ½mv_esc² = GMm/r → v_esc = √(2GM/r).

points.label: For Earth
points.text: v_esc = √2 × v_orb = 11.2 km/s. Rockets must exceed this (after accounting for air resistance, real speed is higher).

slides.inSimpleWords: Orbital speed keeps you circling Earth (7.9 km/s). Escape velocity is √2 times faster (11.2 km/s)—enough to leave Earth's gravity forever.

slides.title: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion
slides.storyContext: Neha pulls out a diagram of the solar system: 'Planets don't orbit in perfect circles. They follow ellipses. And their speeds aren't constant. Kepler discovered three laws that describe this.'

points.label: Kepler's 1st Law
points.text: Each planet orbits the Sun in an ellipse, with the Sun at one focus (not the center).

points.label: Kepler's 2nd Law
points.text: A line from the Sun to a planet sweeps equal areas in equal times. Planets move faster near the Sun (perihelion) and slower far away (aphelion).

points.label: Kepler's 3rd Law
points.text: T² ∝ r³ (orbital period squared is proportional to semi-major axis cubed). T² / r³ = 4π² / (GM) = constant for all planets around the same star.

points.label: Example
points.text: Mercury (r ≈ 0.39 AU) has T ≈ 0.24 years. Mars (r ≈ 1.52 AU) has T ≈ 1.88 years. Check: (0.24² / 0.39³) ≈ (1.88² / 1.52³) ✓

slides.inSimpleWords: Planets orbit in ellipses (not circles). They move faster when close to the Sun and slower when far. Kepler's 3rd law ties orbital period to distance.

slides.title: Gravitational Potential Energy & Total Energy
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma derives: 'The potential energy at distance r from mass M is PE = −GMm/r. Negative, because we measure it relative to infinity.'

points.label: Gravitational PE
points.text: PE = −GMm/r (negative because gravity is attractive). At r = ∞, PE = 0. At Earth's surface, PE = −GMm/R < 0.

points.label: Total energy in orbit
points.text: E_total = KE + PE = ½mv² − GMm/r. For circular orbit: v = √(GM/r), so E = −GMm/(2r). Negative, meaning bound orbit.

points.label: Escape criterion
points.text: For an object to escape (reach r = ∞ with v = 0), E_total ≥ 0. Below Earth's surface at ground level, E = ½m(11.2 km/s)² − GMm/R = 0 at escape velocity.

points.label: Bound vs unbound
points.text: E < 0: bound (circular or elliptical orbit). E = 0: parabolic trajectory (just barely escapes). E > 0: hyperbolic (unbound, moving away permanently).

slides.inSimpleWords: Gravitational PE is negative (you're trapped in the potential well). Total energy = KE + PE determines whether you escape (E ≥ 0) or stay bound (E < 0).

slides.title: Black Holes & Event Horizons (Bonus Physics)
slides.storyContext: Advaith dreams big: 'What if gravity gets so strong that light can't escape?' Dr. Sharma nods: 'That's a black hole. The escape velocity reaches the speed of light.'

points.label: Schwarzschild radius
points.text: A black hole forms when a massive object is compressed. The event horizon radius is R_s = 2GM/c² (c = speed of light ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s).

points.label: For Earth
points.text: If Earth were compressed: R_s = 2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6 × 10²⁴ / (9 × 10¹⁶) ≈ 9 mm. Earth as a marble-sized black hole!

points.label: For the Sun
points.text: R_s ≈ 3 km. The Sun compressed to 3 km radius becomes a black hole.

points.label: At the event horizon
points.text: Escape velocity = c. Once inside, not even light escapes. The singularity at the center has infinite density (in classical physics).

slides.inSimpleWords: Black holes are so dense that their escape velocity equals the speed of light. Nothing can escape, not even photons. The boundary is called the event horizon.

slides.title: Worked Example: Satellite Orbit
slides.storyContext: A satellite orbits Earth at altitude h = 400 km (like the ISS). Find orbital speed and orbital period.

example.problem: Satellite at altitude h = 400 km above Earth (R_earth = 6400 km, M_earth = 6 × 10²⁴ kg). Find (1) orbital speed and (2) period.
example.solution: Step 1: Orbital radius r = R + h = 6400 + 400 = 6800 km = 6.8 × 10⁶ m. Step 2: Orbital speed v = √(GM/r) = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6 × 10²⁴ / 6.8 × 10⁶) ≈ 7680 m/s ≈ 7.68 km/s. Step 3: Period T = 2πr/v = 2π × 6.8 × 10⁶ / 7680 ≈ 5560 seconds ≈ 92.7 minutes ≈ 1.55 hours.

slides.inSimpleWords: The ISS orbits Earth at 7.68 km/s and completes one orbit every 92.7 minutes (about 1.5 hours). Astronauts see 16 sunrises and sunsets per day!

slides.title: Your Turn: Finding Escape Velocity from the Moon
slides.storyContext: Advaith wonders: 'On the Moon, can I jump to space?' (Moon mass M_moon = 7.3 × 10²², radius R_moon = 1.7 × 10⁶ m.)

example.problem: Find escape velocity from the Moon's surface.
example.solution: v_esc = √(2GM/R) = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 7.3 × 10²² / 1.7 × 10⁶) = √(9.73 × 10¹² / 1.7 × 10⁶) ≈ √(5.72 × 10⁶) ≈ 2.39 km/s. Only 2.39 km/s (vs Earth's 11.2 km/s)! A rocket jumping at 2.4 km/s would escape the Moon—but astronauts can't jump that fast.

slides.inSimpleWords: The Moon's escape velocity is 2.4 km/s—weaker gravity than Earth. Astronauts couldn't jump to space, but a good throw might reach escape velocity!

slides.title: What You've Learned
slides.storyContext: The night has grown late. Advaith dreams of rockets and distant stars. Dr. Sharma closes: 'Gravity stitches the cosmos together. One law, infinite beauty.'

points.text: Newton's law: F = Gm₁m₂/r². Gravity is mutual, universal, and weakens with distance squared.
Gravitational field g = GM/r² determines acceleration in space. Same g affects all objects equally.
Orbital speed v_orb = √(GM/r); Escape velocity v_esc = √(2GM/r). Escape velocity is √2 times orbital speed.
Kepler's 3 laws describe planetary orbits: ellipses, equal-area sweeps, T² ∝ r³.
Total energy E = KE + PE = −GMm/(2r) for circular orbits. Negative energy means bound orbit.
Black holes form when mass is compressed within Schwarzschild radius R_s = 2GM/c². Escape velocity reaches c.

slides.inSimpleWords: Gravity is the universe's most fundamental force. It holds planets in orbit, shapes galaxies, and in extreme cases creates black holes. One equation, infinite implications.
